question.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})$ and the denominator $v(x)={x}^{3}+2.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=\frac{3}{x},\,{v}^{′}(x)=3{x}^{2}.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{x})({x}^{3}+2)-(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}))(3{x}^{2})}{({x}^{3}+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3({x}^{3}+2)-3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})}{x({x}^{3}+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}-3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})+6}{x({x}^{3}+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
